population.note: City-proper and DFW-metro figures are approximate mid-2020s estimates pending Census reconciliation; DFW is a genuinely polycentric metro (Fort Worth, Arlington, Plano, etc. are independent city governments, not annexed Dallas territory), which is a different fragmentation mechanism than OKC's aggressive-annexation pattern noted in that city's file. No fragmentation ratio has been computed here — left null rather than guessed.

visitWindow.note: Trip 1 stop between Oklahoma City and Austin; guide built retroactively as control-group data against Trip 2's sourced-curation cities.

framing: A city that rebuilt itself twice on erasure: Freedman's Town, the roughly 276-acre Black community northeast of downtown founded by formerly enslaved people starting in 1869, was severed by Central Expressway in the 1940s and finished off by Woodall Rodgers Freeway in 1962 -- its cemetery is now a strip of historical markers next to a Walmart, and the district itself is Uptown Dallas condos. A second freedman's town, Tenth Street in Oak Cliff, was cut in half by I-35 and has lost roughly a quarter of its historic homes since, currently on the National Trust's most-endangered list. Sourced curation surfaces both; self-curation almost certainly surfaces Dealey Plaza, the Sixth Floor Museum, and not much else about the city's Black history. Deep Ellum runs the opposite arc -- a Black commercial and jazz corridor gutted by the same highway era that produced, decades later, an organic 1980s DIY punk scene (Butthole Surfers, Reverend Horton Heat, Erykah Badu) built in the same abandoned warehouses.

analyticalThread.summary: Freedman's Town (Uptown/State-Thomas) is this city's anchor instance: a post-emancipation Black business and residential district of roughly 276 acres, founded 1869, severed by Central Expressway construction in the 1940s (which was later discovered to have been built directly atop Freedman's Cemetery, undisturbed until a 1990s expansion) and finished off by Woodall Rodgers Freeway in 1962. A second, distinct instance -- Tenth Street Freedman's Town in Oak Cliff, cut in half by I-35 and currently on the National Trust for Historic Preservation's most-endangered list, with roughly 70 of 260 historic homes already demolished -- runs the same mechanism (highway construction over organic decline) inside the same city, which is itself a notable finding: Dallas didn't erase one Black business district, it erased at least two by the same method.

locations.name: Dallas City Hall
locations.note: I.M. Pei's inverted-pyramid municipal building doubled as OCP Headquarters and the Detroit police station exterior. Free to view from the plaza.

locations.name: Dealey Plaza
locations.note: Shot on the actual assassination site. The grassy knoll, the X marks on Elm St, and the Texas School Book Depository (now the Sixth Floor Museum) are all still there and free to walk.

locations.name: Texas Theatre
locations.note: Oak Cliff's restored 1931 theater, now an independent repertory cinema -- doubles as the film's title location and as the real site where Lee Harvey Oswald was arrested on Nov 22, 1963.

locations.name: Dallas metro area
locations.note: Anderson's directorial debut, shot around Dallas where he grew up; an early template for the visual style he'd refine through his career.

correctionNote.text: The TV series Dallas (1978-91, and its 2012 reboot) is the single most commonly assumed Dallas filming credit, but its signature location, Southfork Ranch, is in Parker, TX -- roughly 25 miles north of downtown Dallas, not within city limits. It's still a real, visitable tourist attraction (working ranch plus a Dallas TV series museum) -- just not an in-city stop.
correctionNote.citedFrom: General knowledge -- verify against current Southfork Ranch visitor info before relying on hours/pricing

notablePeople.name: Stevie Ray Vaughan
notablePeople.note: Blues guitar legend, raised in Oak Cliff; a statue of him stands in Kiest Park.
notablePeople.citedFrom: Wikipedia -- List of people from Dallas

notablePeople.name: Erykah Badu
notablePeople.note: Neo-soul icon raised in South Dallas (Roseland Homes area, itself built over part of Freedman's Town); explicitly political lyrics and community organizing ties to South Dallas remain active.

notablePeople.name: Dimebag Darrell
notablePeople.note: Pantera guitarist; DFW's most significant contribution to heavy/hardcore-adjacent music, murdered onstage in 2004.
notablePeople.citedFrom: Wikipedia -- List of people from Dallas

notablePeople.name: Gibby Haynes
notablePeople.note: Butthole Surfers frontman; noise-punk provocateur whose band became one of the defining acts of the Deep Ellum-adjacent Texas underground, though the band itself formed in San Antonio.
notablePeople.citedFrom: Wikipedia -- List of people from Dallas

notablePeople.name: Terry Southern
notablePeople.note: Screenwriter (Dr. Strangelove, Easy Rider) and novelist central to 1960s countercultural satire; birthplace attribution varies by source -- verify before publication.

notablePeople.name: Lee Harvey Oswald
notablePeople.note: Assassinated JFK from the Texas School Book Depository, Nov 22, 1963; captured hours later at the Texas Theatre. Included here as unavoidable, load-bearing Dallas history, not as an endorsement -- the Sixth Floor Museum's framing is worth comparing against Dealey Plaza's freelance conspiracy vendors on the plaza itself.

recommendations.name: Pan-African Connection
recommendations.note: A 37-year Black-owned institution -- gallery, resource center, and bookstore in one -- stocking African and African-American history, art, and banned books, with a stated mission that 'Black history did not start in slavery, but in Africa.' The closest thing Dallas has to the mandatory infoshop pick; see the honest gap below on why a true anarchist storefront doesn't exist here.

recommendations.name: Deep Vellum Books
recommendations.note: Indie bookstore attached to Deep Vellum's own nonprofit press, which specializes in small-press works, translations, and authors of color. Coffee shop on site plus a steady calendar of readings and open mics.

recommendations.name: The Wild Detectives
recommendations.note: Bookstore-cafe-bar hybrid founded in 2014 by two Spanish civil engineers; hosts readings, music, tastings, and film screenings in the same room you're browsing in.

recommendations.name: Crow Hollow Bookshop
recommendations.district: Allen, TX (DFW metro, ~30 min north of downtown Dallas)
recommendations.note: A genre-specialty shop built around horror, thriller, mystery, and science fiction -- the sharpest horror-literature pick in the metro, though it's a DFW-suburb detour rather than an in-Dallas stop.

recommendations.name: Half Price Books Flagship Store
recommendations.note: The founding store of the now-national used-book chain, launched in Dallas in 1972 out of a former laundromat; the flagship carries books, vinyl, and movies at a scale worth the detour on its own. Atlas Obscura listed.

source.detail: Atlas Obscura -- Half Price Books Flagship Store

recommendations.name: Good Records
recommendations.note: A beloved East Dallas institution and hub for local musicians, running the long-standing 'Live From the Astroturf' in-store performance series that's hosted St. Vincent, They Might Be Giants, and Alice Cooper.

recommendations.name: Top Ten Records
recommendations.note: Dallas's oldest record store, which formally became an arts and culture nonprofit in 2016 -- now functions as a music library and archive where you can check out and listen to rare pressings in-store.

recommendations.name: Spinster Records
recommendations.address: 408 N Bishop Ave, Suite 102, Dallas, TX 75208
recommendations.note: Regularly hosts in-store performances, book signings, panels, and pop-up events -- a working community room as much as a record shop.

recommendations.name: GROWL
recommendations.district: Arlington (DFW metro, ~25 min from downtown Dallas)
recommendations.note: Part record store, part comic shop, part live venue -- a genuine haven for punk collectors who 'love their music loud and their culture raw.' Worth the drive out of Dallas proper.

recommendations.name: Josey Records
recommendations.address: 2821 Lyndon B Johnson Fwy, Farmers Branch, TX 75234
recommendations.note: A 25,000-square-foot warehouse run by and for vinyl nerds -- one of the largest single-location inventories in the region.

recommendations.name: Full City Rooster
recommendations.note: A local roasting studio doing small-batch, single-origin roasts out of a working roastery cafe, with almond croissants worth pairing.

recommendations.name: Noble Coyote Coffee Roasters
recommendations.note: Local roaster with an on-site cafe near Fair Park -- pairs naturally with a Sights-category stop at the fairgrounds.

recommendations.name: Be Kinder Coffee
recommendations.note: Nonprofit cafe providing refugees with a safe space, job-skills training, and access to English classes -- the strongest political-bent pick in Dallas coffee. Known for cold brew and homemade granola.

recommendations.name: Houndstooth Coffee
recommendations.note: Named the 'most beautiful coffee shop in Texas' by Architectural Digest; serves Tweed Coffee Roasters in a striking minimalist space.

recommendations.name: Davis Street Espresso
recommendations.note: Deliberately no WiFi and no to-go cups -- an Italian-espresso-bar ethos that asks you to sit down and actually drink the coffee.

recommendations.name: Kessler Baking Studio
recommendations.bestTime: Saturday morning for the cinnamon rolls
recommendations.note: Owner is a James Beard semifinalist; 'Cinnamon Roll Saturdays' is a genuine local institution worth timing a visit around.

recommendations.name: Empire Baking Co.
recommendations.address: 3700 McKinney Ave, Dallas, TX 75204 (plus two other locations)
recommendations.note: One of Dallas's longest-standing craft bakeries, operating since 1992 -- a benchmark for daily bread as much as pastry.

recommendations.name: Oak Cliff Bread
recommendations.note: Small-batch, rotating weekly menu of sourdough, focaccia, and French baguettes; sandwiches served Thu-Fri at 11:30am only. Genuinely limited-run, not a padded pick.

recommendations.name: La Casita Bakeshop
recommendations.address: 580 W Arapaho Rd, Richardson, TX / 5801 E Northwest Hwy, Dallas, TX
recommendations.note: Churro cruffins and a daily rotating case that reliably sells out. The Northwest Highway location flips into a tiki bar after 5pm.

recommendations.name: Chelles Macarons
recommendations.note: Unusual flavor combinations, Raspberry Rose among the standouts -- a good mailable-adjacent pick for boxed sets, though best eaten fresh.

recommendations.name: Frozen Margarita
recommendations.bestTime: Any time, but it's a happy-hour institution
recommendations.note: Invented in Dallas in 1971 by Mariano Martinez, who adapted a 7-Eleven Slurpee machine to keep margaritas at pour-ready consistency -- the original machine now lives in the Smithsonian. A genuine Dallas invention, not a borrowed Tex-Mex staple.

recommendations.name: Fletcher's Original Corny Dog
restaurants: Fletcher's Corny Dogs (State Fair of Texas, Fair Park)
recommendations.bestTime: During State Fair of Texas (late Sept-late Oct) -- check dates against your visit window
recommendations.note: Invented by the Fletcher brothers in 1942, the corn dog on a stick was born at Fair Park and is still sold only during the fair's run -- a genuinely date-gated regional invention.

recommendations.name: Tex-Mex Combo Plate / Queso
recommendations.note: El Fenix opened in 1918 and is credited as one of Texas's first Tex-Mex restaurants -- the combo-plate-and-queso format most people now think of as generically 'Mexican food' has a specific Dallas commercial origin point here.

recommendations.name: Texas Brisket & Burnt Ends
recommendations.note: Pecan Lodge is the highest-profile Deep Ellum barbecue stop, close enough to Deep Vellum Books and Three Links to chain into one afternoon in the neighborhood.

recommendations.name: Chicken-Fried Steak
recommendations.note: The standard Texas diner order; Norma's Cafe has been serving it since 1956 out of the same Oak Lawn location.

recommendations.name: Fxcking Hot Sauces
recommendations.note: Hand-made, locally sourced hot sauce; the Howlin' Wolf blend (smoked habanero, tomatillo) is the standout.

recommendations.name: Poor Vida 'Mixtape' Hot Sauce
recommendations.note: A hip-hop-themed hot sauce line celebrating local Dallas rap culture -- flavors include Texas Pebre and Lemon Pepper Garlic. The closest thing on this list to a music-scene-adjacent food gift.

recommendations.name: Local Honey -- Dallas Farmers Market
recommendations.note: The market's Shed 2 vendor stalls regularly carry North Texas apiary honey alongside Eden Hill Vineyard wine and Mexican-artisan goods -- a reliable one-stop for jarred, mailable gifts.

recommendations.name: Dude, Sweet Chocolate
recommendations.note: Chef Katherine Clapner's bean-to-bar chocolate operation -- barks, truffles, and marshmallows that ship well and travel better than most bakery items.

recommendations.name: Herman Marshall Bourbon / Rye
recommendations.address: 121 N Ballard Ave, Wylie, TX 75098 (DFW metro, ~30 min from downtown Dallas)
recommendations.bestTime: Friday/Saturday night for live music, or any afternoon for a straightforward tasting
recommendations.note: A Texas straight bourbon and rye distillery with a proper tasting room (bingo Tuesdays, trivia Wednesdays, live music weekends) -- worth the drive out for the whiskey/bourbon interest even though it's technically a Wylie address, not Dallas proper.

recommendations.name: Sixth Floor Museum at Dealey Plaza
recommendations.note: Housed in the former Texas School Book Depository, overlooking the actual assassination site. The plaza outside is free and permanently staffed by freelance conspiracy vendors and self-appointed tour guides -- worth 20 minutes on its own before or instead of the paid museum.

recommendations.name: Freedman's Memorial Cemetery & Park
recommendations.district: Uptown / North Central Expressway at Lemmon Ave
recommendations.note: The physical anchor of the Freedman's Town thread: the cemetery of the post-emancipation community founded here in 1869, discovered in the late 1980s to have been built over directly by the 1940s North Central Expressway. Bronze memorial sculptures and historical markers now sit steps from a Walmart -- itself part of the story.

recommendations.name: Knights of Pythias Temple (The Pittman Hotel)
recommendations.note: Designed in 1916 by William Sydney Pittman, the first professionally trained Black architect in Texas and Booker T. Washington's son-in-law -- once among the only Black-owned commercial high-rises in the segregated South. Restored and reopened in 2021 as a boutique hotel bearing Pittman's name; verify current public-access policy before counting on an interior look.

source.detail: General knowledge -- verify address and current operator before publishing

recommendations.name: Texas Theatre
recommendations.bestTime: Evening -- check the repertory calendar for horror programming
recommendations.note: Opened 1931, the first air-conditioned theater in Dallas; site of Lee Harvey Oswald's 1963 capture, now an independent two-screen repertory cinema under Aviation Cinemas with regular horror and cult programming.

recommendations.name: The Traveling Man
recommendations.district: Deep Ellum (DART Green Line, Deep Ellum Station)
recommendations.bestTime: Anytime, but best photographed at golden hour
recommendations.note: Three enormous steel figures depicting 'the emergence of a giant robot born of a locomotive and spilled gin' -- pure outsider-art strangeness planted right at a DART stop in the same neighborhood as most of this guide's punk venues.

recommendations.name: Outlaw Graves -- Bonnie Parker & Clyde Barrow
recommendations.district: Crown Hill Memorial Park (Bonnie) / Western Heights Cemetery (Clyde), Dallas
recommendations.duration: 45 min combined (two separate cemeteries, ~15 min apart by car)
recommendations.note: Bonnie and Clyde are buried in two different Dallas cemeteries, not side by side as popular myth has it -- Bonnie's family wouldn't allow it. Both Atlas Obscura listed and a genuinely strange true-crime pilgrimage.

recommendations.name: White Rock Lake
recommendations.note: A 1,254-acre lake and park entirely inside Dallas city limits -- the natural-attraction balance-rule pick that doesn't require leaving the city, with a 9.3-mile trail loop, kayak rentals, and a bird sanctuary at its east end.

recommendations.name: Meow Wolf Grapevine
recommendations.district: Grapevine, TX (DFW metro, ~35 min from downtown Dallas)
recommendations.note: A trippy, 30+ room immersive art installation about a missing suburban family, with portals to alternate dimensions built by working artists -- the DIY-maker aesthetic scaled up to an attraction, though it's a DFW-suburb trip rather than in-city.

recommendations.name: Three Links
recommendations.note: A perfectly sized DIY-scaled stage with cheap drink specials -- the small-room punk-and-indie standby of Deep Ellum.

recommendations.name: Club Dada
recommendations.note: A long-standing Deep Ellum anchor venue with a low stage and a big multilevel back patio -- sometimes runs two shows a night.

recommendations.name: Fabrication Yard
recommendations.note: A genuinely underground, generator-powered DIY venue down dirt roads among tagged industrial buildings -- the least institutional pick in this category by design.

recommendations.name: GROWL
recommendations.note: The same record-store-slash-venue from Category 2, worth a second mention here as a genuine all-ages DIY show space.

recommendations.name: Double Wide
recommendations.note: Trailer-themed dive bar that explicitly allows moshing, home of the Dallas-famous Yoohoo YeeHaw shot -- unpretentious and loud.

recommendations.name: We Are 1976
recommendations.note: A letterpress shop selling witty cards, posters, and art pieces designed by local artists -- a real alternative to a mass-market magnet.

recommendations.name: Bullzerk
recommendations.note: Dallas-based apparel brand doing hand-printed, original designs with a wry, DIY sensibility.

recommendations.name: Mosaic Makers Collective
recommendations.note: Apparel, home goods, accessories, and paper goods handmade entirely by Texan women artisans.

recommendations.name: Half Price Books Flagship (books & vinyl as souvenirs)
recommendations.note: The Dallas-founded flagship again -- a Texas-published book or a used vinyl find makes a more meaningful souvenir than a magnet.

source.detail: Atlas Obscura -- Half Price Books Flagship Store

recommendations.name: Dallas Farmers Market
recommendations.note: Local honey, Eden Hill Vineyard wine, and Mexican-artisan goods sit alongside produce stalls -- a one-stop for edible souvenirs that also cross-lists with the gifts category.

recommendations.name: Dallas Makerspace
recommendations.district: Carrollton (DFW metro, ~25 min from downtown Dallas)
recommendations.note: A 36,000-square-foot nonprofit community workshop with dedicated electronics, robotics, and laser/engraving areas -- the region's flagship makerspace, with a standing Saturday-morning open house for non-members.

recommendations.name: Tone Shop Guitars
recommendations.note: Billed as DFW's premier guitar store -- a solid stop for pedal demos and gear-hacking supplies even without a dedicated synth shop in the metro.

recommendations.name: SoloDallas
recommendations.note: A Dallas-based boutique effects-pedal manufacturer specializing in Uni-Vibe-style modulation circuits used by prog and classic-rock guitarists -- primarily an online operation; confirm whether a walk-in showroom currently exists before planning around it.

recommendations.name: Mouser Electronics (HQ)
recommendations.note: One of the largest electronic-component distributors in the world is headquartered in the DFW metro -- not a place to visit, but a genuinely relevant fact for anyone doing hardware-hacking who's wondered where their parts orders ship from.

statusNotes.text: Knights of Pythias Temple / The Pittman Hotel address and current public-access policy were not independently confirmed via a live fetch this run -- verify before publishing or visiting.
SoloDallas's walk-in showroom status is unconfirmed; the business may be online/appointment-only. Call ahead.
Southfork Ranch (the TV series Dallas's signature location) is in Parker, TX, about 25 miles north of downtown -- not an in-city stop, despite being the most commonly assumed Dallas filming credit.

honestGaps.text: The mandatory anarchist/radical/infoshop search turned up a DFW Anarchist Bookfair (an annual event, not a storefront) and no permanent walk-in infoshop in Dallas proper. Pan-African Connection is the closest sustained political-bookstore anchor the city has -- a Black-nationalist community institution rather than an anarchist one. Worth comparing against OKC's finding that red-state metros tend to produce cooperative and community-institution infrastructure where coastal cities produce infoshops; Dallas's version leans further still toward a single legacy institution rather than either model.

No dedicated synthesizer retailer was found in Dallas or the wider DFW metro -- a Gearspace forum thread on the exact question confirms the gap, noting only Guitar Center locations and a now-closed local retailer (Brook Mays). Category 10 leans on a general-purpose makerspace, a guitar/pedal shop, and a boutique pedal maker instead of padding in a synth store that doesn't exist.

scopeDecision: Dallas-proper primary; several picks (GROWL in Arlington, Herman Marshall in Wylie, Dallas Makerspace in Carrollton, Meow Wolf in Grapevine, Crow Hollow Bookshop in Allen) reach into the wider DFW metro where the category genuinely couldn't be answered as well in-city -- each is flagged with its district/distance rather than presented as an in-Dallas stop.
